segments.title: Tiger's beam leaves room to consider larger barbettes
segments.body: Tiger's 13.5-inch barbettes were about 24 feet 6 inches across, while the 15-inch Mark I mounting required roughly 30 feet. The diameter would have to grow by 5 feet 6 inches, or 2 feet 9 inches on each side. Tiger's beam was 90 feet 6 inches, only an inch narrower than the Queen Elizabeth class, which already carried 15-inch guns. Their similar beams give a first reason to investigate whether Tiger could accommodate the larger mountings.

evidence.note: Gives both barbette diameters, the required enlargement, and the nearly identical beams of Tiger and the Queen Elizabeth class.

segments.summary: The proposed gun change requires wider barbettes, and Tiger's beam is almost identical to that of the 15-inch-armed Queen Elizabeth class.

segments.title: A rough hull comparison puts Tiger near existing 15-inch ships
segments.body: A rough comparison divides standard displacement by half the product of length and beam. Using the figures in the discussion gives the Queen Elizabeth class about 0.9489, Tiger 0.8947, Renown 0.7405, and Hood about 0.9190. Tiger's 28,500-ton standard displacement puts her much closer on this measure to ships already carrying 15-inch guns than to Renown. The figures are a quick comparison of how heavily the ships were built, with substantial reconstruction still required. They support an initial case for carrying the larger armament.

evidence.note: Explains the calculation and gives the comparative figures for Queen Elizabeth, Tiger, Renown, and Hood.
Uses the comparison to support rearmament while acknowledging the work required.

segments.summary: Displacement divided by approximate hull area supplies a rough comparison for judging whether Tiger could support heavier guns.

segments.title: Tiger approaches the fast battleship from the battlecruiser side
segments.body: Tiger represents one side of a British design convergence toward the fast battleship. Battlecruisers develop toward Tiger while battleships develop toward the Queen Elizabeth class, producing ships that solve similar speed-and-protection problems from different starting points. Hood looks denser on a simple displacement calculation, but much of her protection was added after Jutland while she was already under construction. Tiger's internal structure was designed as a coherent, heavily built package from the outset. The comparison shows how labels can conceal the fast-battleship qualities of some late battlecruisers.

evidence.note: Describes battlecruiser and battleship development as two British routes toward the fast battleship.
Contrasts Tiger's purpose-built density with protection added to Hood after Jutland.

segments.summary: Tiger and the Queen Elizabeth class represent two British routes toward combining battle-line strength with high speed.

segments.title: Tiger's trials and stability suggest scope for an oil-fired refit
segments.body: Tiger's official speed was 28 knots, while her fully laden trials reached about 29.5 knots. Her machinery used 39 coal-and-oil-fired boilers at 235 psi in five rooms, four with eight boilers and one with seven. Full oil firing could plausibly have brought her to about 30 knots. Her metacentric height at deep load was about 6 feet, or 1.9 metres, which is presented as a reason for her stability. These are useful starting points for the refit proposal, with the higher speed remaining an estimate.

evidence.note: Gives official and trial speeds, boiler pressure, mixed firing, the oil-fired estimate, and the boiler-room arrangement.
Gives metacentric height at deep load and describes Tiger as stable.

segments.summary: Trials speed, the 39-boiler plant, and deep-load stability provide the starting figures for Tiger's proposed machinery upgrade.

segments.title: Tiger adds substantial weight to a hull only slightly larger than Queen Mary's
segments.body: Tiger was only about 4 feet longer and roughly 1.5 feet wider than Queen Mary, yet she was about 2,000 tons heavier. The extra weight marks a substantial design difference despite the similar dimensions. British planners were watching German construction and Japan's Kongo-class orders, alongside wider discussion of battlecruiser development. Encounters between opposing battlecruisers looked increasingly likely, while faster battle-line designs were also under discussion. Those pressures help explain Tiger's move toward the qualities of a fast battleship.

evidence.note: Queen Mary, German construction, and Japan's Kongo class explain why Tiger's designers invested in a heavier ship.

segments.summary: Queen Mary, German construction, and Japan's Kongo class explain why Tiger's designers invested in a heavier ship.

segments.title: Jutland supplies combat evidence for Tiger's resilience
segments.body: At Jutland, Tiger was hit by fifteen 11-inch shells, at least two 12-inch shells, and several 5.9-inch rounds. Damage affected her belt area, flare stores, and sick bay, with a cable locker also recalled as a possible damaged space. A funnel is tentatively described as having been heavily peppered. Despite the punishment, Tiger survived and returned to service quickly. Her resilience helps explain why the Royal Navy wanted to retain her at Washington, and supplies combat experience relevant to the proposed reconstruction.

evidence.note: Enumerates Tiger's shell hits and damaged spaces, with the cable locker recalled tentatively.
Describes rapid return to service, tentatively recalls funnel damage, and connects resilience to British interest in retaining Tiger at Washington.

segments.summary: Tiger's heavy shell damage and rapid return to service provide a wartime test of the hull strength assumed by the refit scenario.

segments.title: Washington treaty rules block the historical Tiger gun change
segments.body: Technical feasibility and treaty permission were separate questions. The reconstruction rules permitted bulges, blisters, anti-aircraft deck protection, and up to 3,000 tons of defensive additions. They generally barred changes to side armor and to the caliber, number, or general mounting type of a retained capital ship's main armament. France and Italy could increase armor protection and gun caliber within the stated allowance, up to the 16-inch limit. Britain's named Renown exception covered armor alterations already begun and temporarily suspended. Tiger could remain below the 35,000-ton standard-displacement ceiling and 16-inch gun limit after a substantial rebuild, yet the specific main-armament prohibition still blocked her conversion. A comparable exception would therefore have needed to be negotiated for Tiger.

evidence.note: Reads the treaty's defensive-reconstruction allowance and prohibition on main-armament changes.
Explains that Tiger met the overall tonnage and caliber limits but failed the reconstruction rule.

segments.summary: Tiger fits the treaty's broad tonnage and caliber ceilings, but the reconstruction clause forbids changing her main-gun caliber or mounting type.

segments.title: Stored Courageous turrets show Britain's measured rearmament pace
segments.body: The 15-inch guns and four turrets removed during the Courageous-class carrier conversions were stored, leaving the main hardware for an eight-gun ship available. Britain therefore had equipment that could support an earlier Vanguard-like capital ship. Armor-production limits remained, but Britain also held armor plate in reserve and could buy material abroad, with Sweden and the Czechs named as options. Those resources support the argument that British rearmament followed a chosen political and economic pace. Greater urgency within the armed forces coexisted with political leaders' desire to limit economic strain. In this interpretation, the unused hardware weakens the description of rearmament as a panicked effort to mobilize every available resource.

evidence.note: Raises the fate of Courageous-class 15-inch guns and describes stored armament for a complete ship.
Identifies four stored turrets, acknowledges armor-production limits and foreign supply options, and argues that rearmament was politically measured.

segments.summary: Stored 15-inch mountings from the Courageous-class conversions provide the hardware for an eight-gun ship and weaken claims of panicked rearmament.

segments.title: Internal supports determine how much armor a hull can carry
segments.body: A fully armored battlecruiser could have extensive external armor while retaining a battlecruiser's internal arrangement. Tiger's denser construction provides the closer comparison for the design discussed here. More subdivision, thicker internal metalwork, and additional supports allow a hull to carry greater armor weight. The analogy is hanging a heavy mirror: the structure behind the wall must support the load. Assessing the armor therefore also means examining the hull beneath it.

evidence.note: Distinguishes internal battlecruiser construction from full external armor coverage.
Explains how subdivision, thicker metalwork, and supports carry armor weight, using a heavy mirror analogy.

segments.summary: Subdivision and strong internal construction provide support for heavier external armor.

segments.title: Tiger's strategic speed could put heavy guns at Singapore in time
segments.body: Tiger's 1918 refit and continued retention fit the Royal Navy's worldwide response problem. British political and economic thinking treated the empire as a national necessity, leaving much of its Far Eastern defense to the navy. At a crisis cruising speed near 24 knots, a fast squadron could reach Singapore from Portsmouth in about fourteen days or from Malta in roughly ten. The slower battle fleet, advancing at about 18 to 21 knots, is estimated to need twenty-one days or more from Portsmouth. A hypothetical Japanese assault from Sasebo involved about seven days of steaming, with visible mobilization potentially giving another three or four days' warning. Fast ships already at Malta could therefore arrive in time if ordered to sail immediately. Their immediate purpose was deterrence through a visible naval presence while the larger fleet followed.

evidence.note: Introduces Tiger's 1918 refit and compares fast-squadron transit times from Portsmouth and Malta with the battle fleet.
Relates Japanese mobilization warning to Singapore timing and describes the fast ships as a deterrent rapid-response force.

segments.summary: Transit-time arithmetic shows why fast capital ships served as a deterrent and rapid-response force for Britain's Far Eastern commitments.

segments.title: The London treaty removes Tiger before her replacement is ready
segments.body: Tiger remained in commission until 1931 under her final captain, Arthur Bedford. Her withdrawal followed the London Naval Treaty and British plans to free tonnage for the next generation of capital ships. The replacement program then suffered repeated delays before work began on the King George V class. Tiger was sold for breaking in 1932, although accounts differ on when physical dismantling started. Treaty accounting had therefore removed an existing capability well before its planned replacement reached the fleet.

evidence.note: Connects Tiger's 1931 withdrawal with the London treaty, replacement tonnage, and delays to the King George V class.
Dates the sale for breaking and notes uncertainty over when dismantling actually began.

segments.summary: Tiger left service in 1931 as treaty tonnage was cleared for a new generation, but delays postponed the King George V class and left a capability gap.

segments.title: Frederick Field links design policy to worldwide force projection
segments.body: A plausible Tiger counterfactual needs a reason for naval policy to change. Frederick Field's three years as Third Sea Lord gave him time to develop a longer view, whereas predecessors' brief appointments left less opportunity to settle policy. His preference for F3 over N3 is tied to the possibility of a future war far from Britain. Such a war would require heavy ships able to project power worldwide at speed. That strategic preference supplies an institutional reason to consider retaining and improving Tiger.

evidence.note: Calls for a logical mechanism behind counterfactual change and contrasts brief appointments with Field's three-year tenure.
Connects Field's F3 preference over N3 with distant-war requirements and worldwide force projection.

segments.summary: Field's longer tenure and preference for F3 provide a policy setting in which a faster, more heavily armed Tiger could make sense.

segments.title: Why battlecruisers traded protection for strategic speed
segments.body: A force arriving after a crisis has been decided cannot compensate by being stronger on paper. Forward basing enough battleships could reduce that problem, but it would require substantially more ships and money. Battlecruisers offered another way to move heavy naval power quickly between distant commitments. A fully armored fast battleship became viable only when machinery had enough power density to combine speed with armor and adequate subdivision. Until then, protection required compromises, particularly in how much of the hull the armor covered. Thick armor over a restricted area was different from the fuller coverage associated with a fully armored battlecruiser.

evidence.note: Strategic speed offered an alternative to expensive permanent forward deployment, while machinery limits constrained protection.

segments.summary: Strategic speed offered an alternative to expensive permanent forward deployment, while machinery limits constrained protection.

segments.title: Naval memoirs can obscure the work of subordinates
segments.body: One criticism of Chatfield's autobiographies is that they give too little credit to Admiral Henderson. The explanation offered here goes beyond personal self-interest: a leadership culture in which subordinates' credit flows upward can encourage commanders to regard collective achievements as their own. That interpretation leaves room for institutional habits as well as individual motives. It also raises a problem when using memoirs to assess who shaped naval policy, since the senior author's account can minimise the officers working beneath him.

evidence.note: Introduces Chatfield, criticizes his autobiographical treatment of Henderson, and offers upward-flowing institutional credit as a partly charitable explanation.

segments.summary: The criticism of Chatfield's treatment of Henderson raises a question about how command culture shapes autobiographical credit.

segments.title: Dispersed task groups need speed to support one another
segments.body: Roger Backhouse is presented as an officer deeply concerned with the navy's future deployments. The discussion links him and Field with thinking about task groups dispersed around the world. Small forces operating far apart would need to maneuver quickly if they were to reinforce one another. Strategic speed therefore affected the navy's ability to combine ships for an operation as well as its ability to reach a distant crisis.

evidence.note: Backhouse and Field's interest in dispersed forces makes rapid reinforcement a reason to invest in fast capital ships.

segments.summary: Backhouse and Field's interest in dispersed forces makes rapid reinforcement a reason to invest in fast capital ships.

segments.title: A 15-inch standardization bargain changes the treaty path
segments.body: Two political routes could bypass the historical restriction. Britain could claim that Tiger's conversion was already under way and seek treatment similar to Renown, or it could give up 16-inch ambitions in exchange for standardizing future capital ships on the 15-inch gun. Standardization would simplify fleet logistics while surrendering little practical striking power. Either route depends on securing language in the Washington settlement, since the technical case alone could not override the reconstruction rules.

evidence.note: Sets out the 15-inch standardization bargain and the alternative claim that reconstruction was already in progress.

segments.summary: Britain could seek either an exemption for work already begun or a treaty bargain that traded 16-inch prestige for 15-inch fleet commonality.

segments.title: Standard displacement hides Tiger's full-load scale
segments.body: Tiger's 28,500-ton figure is treated here as standard displacement because that is how Britain declared it for the Washington treaty, despite its being labeled normal displacement elsewhere. The argument notes Britain's incentive to keep the declared figure low as a reason to question those alternative descriptions. Adding the 3,000-ton reconstruction allowance would bring the proposed standard displacement to 31,500 tons. Fuel and feed water fall outside standard displacement. A separate calculation starts with the original 28,500-ton figure, adds about 7,000 tons of coal and fuel oil to reach 35,500, then adds feed water to estimate roughly 39,000 to 40,000 tons at full load. For comparison, Renown and Repulse are given as 26,500 tons standard, the Queen Elizabeth class as 27,500, and the R class as 25,750. On those figures, the rebuilt Tiger would remain smaller than Hood but exceed the standard displacement of the other retained British capital ships.

evidence.note: Distinguishes standard from full-load displacement, estimates full load, and uses the treaty declaration to challenge alternative descriptions of the 28,500-ton figure.
Gives Renown and Repulse's displacement, calculates 31,500 tons after the allowance, and compares Tiger with Hood, the Queen Elizabeth class, and the R class.

segments.summary: Treaty figures omit fuel and feed water, so Tiger's declared 28,500 tons can coexist with an estimated 39,000 to 40,000 tons at full load.

segments.title: New boilers reshape Tiger's machinery layout
segments.body: The proposed rebuild includes all-oil firing, rearranged coal-bunker spaces, and possibly new geared turbines. Reducing the funnels could free deck space for 4-inch guns: the UAD illustration uses one funnel, although a reconstruction might retain two. Tiger and Hood's 235 psi boilers provide the starting comparison with the 250 psi Admiralty three-drum boilers associated with Nelson and Rodney. Tiger's 39 boilers supported 85,000 shaft horsepower, while eight boilers in Nelson and Rodney supported 45,000. On that rough comparison, sixteen modern boilers could provide about 90,000 horsepower while occupying less space, despite being individually larger. About 30 knots is suggested as a possible result. The UAD simulation instead used 29.5 knots and performed well in exercises within the game. Its results illustrate the proposal without establishing the performance of a real reconstruction.

evidence.note: Sketches the funnel, oil-firing, bunker, secondary-gun, turbine, and boiler changes.
Compares Tiger's 39 boilers with Nelson and Rodney's plant and estimates the rebuilt ship's power and speed.

segments.summary: Oil firing and Nelson-era boilers could replace Tiger's 39-boiler plant with a much smaller, more powerful arrangement while freeing internal and deck space.

segments.title: Armor coverage matters alongside maximum thickness
segments.body: Tiger carried a 9-inch belt, about half again as thick as the principal protection on Renown and Repulse but below Hood's 12-inch maximum. Maximum thickness alone does not settle which ship had the better scheme because Tiger's belt covered a different proportion of the hull. Her armor was integrated into the design from the beginning, whereas much of Hood's additional protection entered after construction had started. Tiger also had up to 3 inches of deck armor, and her existing 8-to-9-inch barbettes would be replaced as part of the main-gun conversion. The final protection package would depend on whether the political route allowed an agreed pre-treaty rebuild or secured broader concessions during negotiations.

evidence.note: Compares Tiger's belt, armor coverage, deck armor, and barbettes with Renown, Repulse, and Hood.
Links the achievable protection changes to the two proposed treaty routes.

segments.summary: Tiger's 9-inch belt and original structural integration offer a different protection tradeoff from Hood's thicker but later-added armor.

segments.title: A 1918 reconstruction could keep Tiger useful while new designs took shape
segments.body: In the first scenario, Tiger's reconstruction could begin with her 1918 refit to buy time while the Admiral class and successor designs remained unsettled. The Royal Navy wanted Courageous and Glorious out of the battle line quickly, increasing the value of a useful fast ship. Tiger had seen hard wartime service, but most of it was in the North Sea with access to home maintenance facilities. Warspite's continued usefulness supplies a comparison: she was launched in November 1913, just before Tiger in December. Commissioning reverses that order, since Tiger entered service in October 1914 and Warspite in March 1915. Age and war service therefore provide little basis by themselves for dismissing Tiger as a reconstruction candidate.

evidence.note: Relates imperial responsibilities and delayed successor designs to a possible 1918 reconstruction, then discusses Tiger's service and maintenance.
Distinguishes launch dates from commissioning dates in the comparison with Warspite.

segments.summary: Delayed replacement designs and Tiger's age and service condition support treating the 1918 refit as a possible start for rearmament.

segments.title: Four fast ships support a deploy-train-refit cycle
segments.body: Retaining Tiger alongside Hood, Renown, and Repulse would create a four-ship fast force. A usual four-hull model allows one ship at sea, one training or in transit, one in light refit, and one in major refit. Two eight-gun and two six-gun 15-inch ships would give the force more fighting weight, although their differing designs would still require support. New boilers and all-oil firing would probably improve Tiger's endurance for distant operations. Hood and Tiger could then undertake the round-the-world Empire cruise together as the two ships with the greatest visible gun power. Tiger might also receive a more Atlantic-shaped bow during reconstruction, although that remains a suggested modification.

evidence.note: Explains four-hull force generation, two eight-gun and two six-gun ships, and the differing designs within the force.
Suggests improved range, a Hood-Tiger Empire cruise, and a possible Atlantic-style bow.

segments.summary: Tiger provides the fourth hull for sustainable deployments and could join Hood on the Empire cruise after improvements to endurance.

segments.title: Accepting Tiger may be cheaper than reopening the treaty bargain
segments.body: The treaty system accepted some work and ships that already existed, as the treatment of Renown and Hood illustrates. Refusing the proposed Tiger conversion could prompt Britain to leave the agreement or demand a third new 16-inch capital ship, worsening the tonnage arithmetic for other powers. Allowing the reconstruction could therefore become an acceptable compromise. In this scenario Britain would enter the Second World War with four fast 15-inch capital ships, making it easier to release Hood for modernization while Tiger covered some of her assignments. The consequences would depend on Hood's eventual refit and the different operating characteristics of the two ships. Tiger would probably need more than the proposed sixteen boilers to reach Hood's roughly 32 knots, using additional machinery space. Whether that speed justified a larger installation would remain a separate design decision.

evidence.note: Explains treaty acceptance of the status quo and the alternatives Britain could demand if Tiger were refused.
Traces the effect of a fourth fast ship on Tiger's employment and Hood's modernization schedule.

segments.summary: Treaty partners might tolerate a conversion already under way rather than risk British withdrawal or a demand for another new capital ship.

segments.title: Treaty tonnage could produce three or four F3-style capital ships
segments.body: The more ambitious scenario treats 15-inch standardization as a bargaining asset. After removing the four 13.5-inch battleships and upgrading Tiger, Britain would retain a little over 136,000 tons of capital-ship allowance in this calculation. That could accommodate four ships of about 34,000 tons each, provided an F3-derived design could be brought within that figure. Nelson and Rodney's stated 33,800-ton standard displacement supplies a comparison for the arithmetic. Three new ships are judged a more likely negotiated maximum. Four would give Britain eighteen capital ships: four new ships, four older battlecruisers, five Queen Elizabeths, and five R-class battleships. Eight could make at least 28 knots in the expanded scenario, while the three-new-ship alternative would still provide seven fast capital ships.

evidence.note: Calculates the remaining British treaty allowance and the possible three- or four-ship F3 program.

segments.summary: Giving up 16-inch guns could let Britain use its remaining treaty allowance for a larger family of fast 15-inch ships derived from F3 thinking.

segments.title: Tiger could test a 15-inch/50 before the F2 and F3 ships
segments.body: A rebuilt Tiger could test a proposed 15-inch/50 weapon before that armament entered new capital ships. The F2 and F3 concepts were described as fully armored battlecruisers because their protection covered more of the hull, although their subdivision still followed battlecruiser standards. They continued the design path already visible in Tiger, approaching the fast battleship from the battlecruiser side. Tiger would therefore serve as an experimental bridge between an immediate refit and the next generation of British capital ships.

evidence.note: Suggests Tiger as a 15-inch/50 test ship and describes F2 and F3 as continuations of battlecruiser development toward the fast battleship.

segments.summary: Using rebuilt Tiger as a gun test bed links the immediate conversion to British work on fully armored battlecruisers and fast battleships.

segments.title: Two battle lines give Britain worldwide task-group depth
segments.body: A fleet with four F3s and four older battlecruisers would possess something close to two distinct battle lines. The conventional battle fleet could hold concentrated positions while fast ships formed task groups able to move between theaters. Availability matters as much as the headline total: the larger pool makes it realistic to have two or three fast capital ships at sea and another two or three available in port despite training and refit demands. Even the less expansive seven-ship version would generate substantial deployable strength. The difference between 15-inch and 16-inch guns matters less in this argument than the number of heavy, fast hulls an opponent must account for.

evidence.note: Describes two battle lines and the Royal Navy's capacity to generate worldwide task groups.
Connects a seven- or eight-ship fast force with availability, deterrence, and the limited practical difference between 15-inch and 16-inch hits.

segments.summary: Seven or eight fast capital ships create a second operational battle line with enough depth for simultaneous deployment, maintenance, and deterrence.

segments.title: Fleet depth supports faster Queen Elizabeth refits and live raider exercises
segments.body: A deeper fast force creates schedule room for more refits, including a different Queen Elizabeth modernization aimed at additional speed. It also supplies a capital ship that can maneuver freely as the raider during exercises. Hunting such a target would test scouting and interception against a ship trying to evade at maximum speed. Those exercises could improve preparation for wartime searches for commerce raiders.

evidence.note: Links additional fleet depth to more refits, faster Queen Elizabeth modernizations, and exercises against a freely maneuvering high-speed raider.

segments.summary: More fast hulls free older ships for speed-focused modernization and give training fleets realistic high-speed raiders to hunt.

segments.title: A larger fast fleet undermines the German Panzerschiff concept
segments.body: Panzerschiffe retain some logic against Soviet or French forces, although Dunkerque already weakens the French case. Against Britain, Hood, Renown, and Repulse posed a serious existing risk. Adding Tiger and several fast Nelson- or F3-derived ships greatly expands the number of hunters able to catch and outclass German surface raiders. That change could push German planners away from the Panzerschiff concept before the Second World War.

evidence.note: Argues that numerous fast British capital ships make Panzerschiffe less viable and could redirect German development.

segments.summary: Tiger and several fast Nelson- or F3-derived ships would multiply the British hunters able to catch and outgun German Panzerschiffe.

segments.title: Fast battleships alter Mediterranean operations and Denmark Strait
segments.body: In the expanded scenario, faster Nelson-derived ships could spend more time on mobile operations beyond fixed choke points such as Gibraltar. More high-speed capital ships would let British commanders accept greater operational risk and bring heavier forces to battles such as Matapan. Additional availability could also produce a different British force at the Denmark Strait. These are possible consequences of a larger pool of ships capable of 28 knots or more. The operational benefit lies in deployable speed across the fleet, which determines how much strength can reach a distant operation in time.

evidence.note: Contrasts historical choke-point duties and hunting limitations with possible faster deployments and greater strength at Matapan.
Suggests greater availability at Denmark Strait and emphasizes strategic, deployable speed.

segments.summary: A larger pool of 28-knot capital ships changes where Britain can accept risk and which heavy units can reach time-sensitive operations.

segments.title: A tentative King George V alternative uses twelve 15-inch guns
segments.body: Fleet-wide 15-inch standardization could influence the later King George V class as well as Tiger. One tentative alternative is a 28-knot ship with twelve 15-inch guns in four triple turrets. That arrangement might avoid difficulties associated with the historical quadruple mountings. The suggestion extends the counterfactual to later procurement without establishing a completed design.

evidence.note: A proposed four-triple-turret arrangement shows how choosing 15-inch standardization could carry into a later battleship generation.

segments.summary: A proposed four-triple-turret arrangement shows how choosing 15-inch standardization could carry into a later battleship generation.

segments.title: A 24-knot fast force raises the carrier speed requirement
segments.body: The capital-ship counterfactual reaches carrier design because fleet components must operate together. A traditional battle line progresses at about 18 knots, while this fast force would make at least 24. Carriers assigned to it would need enough speed to remain with the formation and provide support. The requirement ties battleship standardization to naval aviation instead of treating the carrier program in isolation.

evidence.note: Explains why carriers would need to keep pace with a fast capital-ship formation progressing at roughly 24 knots rather than an 18-knot battle line.

segments.summary: Carriers supporting the fast capital ships must keep pace with a formation advancing near 24 knots instead of the traditional 18-knot battle line.

segments.title: An eighteen-ship fleet could support another battle squadron
segments.body: Under the expanded treaty bargain, Britain could reach eighteen capital ships because its retained ships averaged about 27,782 tons once the 13.5-inch ships and Nelson and Rodney were set aside, well below the 35,000-ton individual ceiling. That total could support an additional battle squadron, which then raises the question of where to base it. Direct basing at Singapore becomes less attractive once Fascist Italy and Mediterranean tension demand flexibility closer to the Suez route. Trincomalee in Ceylon or Bombay (Mumbai) on India's west coast would signal a visible commitment to Australia, New Zealand, and Britain's Eastern possessions. Ships stationed there could also move through the Arabian Sea, Red Sea, and Suez Canal to reinforce the Mediterranean from an unexpected direction. The basing choice connects imperial defense with European war planning.

evidence.note: Calculates the eighteen-ship fleet and proposes forming another battle squadron.
Considers Trincomalee or western India as bases able to support both Eastern commitments and rapid movement toward the Mediterranean.

segments.summary: Ceylon or western India offers a politically Eastern but operationally flexible base for the extra squadron created by a larger treaty fleet.
